structure.rationale: Chapters follow the life of a trade, as the requester's syllabus asks: first what a bond is (cash flows), then the product family, then how a mandate becomes positions, how orders are executed, who may be traded with and under which limits, how curves/spreads give relative value, how duration/DV01/convexity/carry turn market moves into P&L, how funding/repo/collateral/settlement finance it, how liquidity/data/models establish price, and finally one end-to-end day-in-the-life that reuses every idea, plus a gentle math primer as appendix. Each chapter answers one operational question: what is held, why, how traded, financed, valued, what can lose money, and how exposure is kept within limits. Sources were gathered at the session level (container web access is restricted); page builds should write prose FROM this artifact without new fetches.
structure.audience: Newcomers to fixed income (and engineers or operations staff supporting a fixed-income desk) who want the business and operating picture, explained in plain words.

claims.text: Bond markets quote clean prices (excluding accrued interest) to aid comparison and avoid price jumps on coupon dates; the cash that changes hands at settlement is the dirty price = clean price + accrued interest.

Accrued interest is the portion of the next coupon the seller earned by holding the bond from the last coupon date to settlement; the buyer pays it at settlement and recovers it when the full coupon arrives.
Between coupon dates the dirty price rises as interest accrues, then drops on the coupon date when accrued interest resets to zero — the clean price removes this sawtooth.
Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions: the price is the present value of fixed future cash flows, so a higher discount rate makes those same cash flows worth less today.
A bond trades at par when its coupon equals the market yield for its risk and maturity, at a premium when the coupon is higher, and at a discount when the coupon is lower.

U.S. corporate bond trades have settled T+1 (one business day after trade date) since May 28, 2024, when the SEC's shortened settlement cycle took effect for cash equities, corporate debt and unit investment trusts.
US corporate bonds typically accrue interest on a 30/360 day count (each month 30 days, year 360).

Illustrative: $1,000,000 face, 5% semiannual coupon, last coupon Mar 15, settle Jun 18 → 93 days 30/360 → accrued $12,916.67; clean 102.25 = $1,022,500; dirty = $1,035,416.67; of the $25,000 Sept coupon the buyer nets $12,083.33.
Main sectors: government/rates, investment grade, high yield, municipals, MBS, ABS, derivatives, emerging-market debt; dealers (sell side) make markets for buy-side investors who hold the bonds.

pitfalls: Readers conflate the quoted (clean) price with the cash they will pay — the settlement cash is the dirty price times face/100, not the quoted price.
'Fixed income' is not always fixed: floating-rate notes, TIPS principal, MBS prepayments and callable bonds all have cash flows that move.
Trade date and settlement date are different days; ownership of the coupon accrual follows settlement conventions, not the handshake.

claims.text: Treasury bills are short-term (4 weeks to 1 year) and sold at a discount with no coupon; notes are 2–10 year coupon securities; bonds run 20–30 years; TIPS adjust principal with CPI; all pay semiannual coupons except bills.

The on-the-run issue is the most recently auctioned security of each tenor and serves as the market benchmark; on-the-runs account for roughly two-thirds of Treasury trading volume while all off-the-runs together trade far less.

General obligation municipal bonds are backed by the issuer's full faith, credit and taxing power; revenue bonds are backed only by a specific project's revenue stream; interest on most munis is exempt from federal income tax, letting municipalities borrow more cheaply.

MBS negative convexity comes from the borrower's free prepayment option: when rates fall, refinancing returns principal early (contraction) just when reinvestment rates are worst; when rates rise, prepayments slow and duration extends (extension).
An MBS therefore rises less than a comparable option-free bond when rates fall and can fall more when rates rise.

A repo is economically a collateralized cash loan: securities are sold with an agreement to repurchase at a higher price, the difference being the repo interest; a haircut means posting more collateral than cash received (e.g. $100 of securities for $98 cash = 2% haircut).

In a general-collateral (GC) repo the cash lender accepts any security meeting broad criteria; when a specific security is in demand it trades 'special' and its repo rate drops below the GC rate — the owner of that bond can borrow cash unusually cheaply by lending it.

A CDS has a premium leg (the protection buyer pays a running spread, accrued act/360) and a protection leg (on a credit event — bankruptcy, failure to pay, restructuring — the seller pays par minus recovery); at fair value the two legs' present values are equal.
Since the LIBOR transition (USD LIBOR panels ended June 2023), new USD swaps reference SOFR, a broad measure of the cost of borrowing cash overnight collateralized by Treasuries in the repo market.

pitfalls: Negative convexity is routinely misexplained as 'MBS lose when rates fall' — they still gain, just less than an option-free bond; the loss of upside, not absolute loss, is the point.
Repo 'specialness' confuses newcomers: a LOWER repo rate on a special means the bond is MORE in demand (lenders of the bond accept cheap cash as payment for borrowing it).
Seniority language (senior secured vs senior unsecured vs subordinated) matters only in default — same issuer, very different recoveries.

claims.text: Investment managers allocate block trades across multiple funds/accounts after execution; the allocation defines quantity and destination account for each piece of one executed trade.

A position has several simultaneous 'truths': the front-office (trade-date) view used for risk, the settlement-date view, the custody view at the custodian, and the accounting books and records — reconciliations keep them aligned.

Market value (price × holdings, in cash terms) differs from notional/face value (the contractual principal); P&L splits into realized (from closed lots and received cash flows) and unrealized (mark-to-market on open lots).

pitfalls: Gross vs net exposure: a long $100m and short $90m book is $10m net but $190m gross — risk, funding and balance-sheet costs often follow gross, not net.
Dealer inventory is not free: every bond held must be financed (repo or capital), so 'the desk holds it' always has a running cost.
Encumbered/pledged inventory looks like a holding but cannot be sold or lent — available inventory is what matters for trading decisions.

claims.text: Most fixed income trading is quote-driven and dealer-intermediated rather than order-driven like equities; the dominant electronic protocol is request-for-quote (RFQ), where a client asks several dealers for prices and picks the best response.

Newer protocols widen the liquidity pool: all-to-all trading (e.g. MarketAxess Open Trading) lets investors trade with each other, not only with dealers; portfolio trading prices a whole list of bonds as one package; request-for-stream and auto-execution automate smaller tickets.
An axe is a dealer's advertised, genuine interest to buy or sell a specific bond, usually tied to a risk position they want to offload or cover or a client order they are working.
Investors watch dealer axes because trading with an axed dealer often means executing inside the bid-ask spread and in larger than normal size — the dealer wants the trade, so they pay up for it.

After execution the trade is allocated, then confirmed (the dealer's record of terms) and affirmed (the investor's agreement to that record); central matching platforms like DTCC CTM automate allocation-confirmation-affirmation, and T+1 settlement pushed affirmation to trade date (recommended cutoff 9 PM ET).

Execution records keep timestamps, every dealer's quote and response time, venue, size, partial fills, amendments and the rationale — both for best-execution review and to learn which counterparties actually show up with liquidity.

pitfalls: Indicative quotes are not executable: a dealer run or screen price is an advertisement, and the real price for your size arrives only when you ask.
Sending an RFQ to too many dealers leaks information — the losers learn your intention and the market can move against you before you trade (information leakage).
An axe can be strong or weak; a stale or courtesy axe is not a commitment, which is why response history per dealer is tracked.

claims.text: The ISDA Master Agreement is the standard contract for OTC derivatives between two parties, supplemented by a Schedule, per-trade Confirmations, and a Credit Support Annex; together they allow close-out netting of all trades on default.

The Credit Support Annex turns 'post collateral' into hard numbers: eligible collateral types, valuation and haircuts, thresholds (how much exposure may run uncollateralized), minimum transfer amounts, and call frequency.
Repo trading runs under its own master agreement, the GMRA (Global Master Repurchase Agreement) — the repo analogue of the ISDA MA.

Before any trading relationship starts, onboarding completes KYC/AML review, tax documentation, legal agreements (ISDA/CSA, GMRA, clearing and custody agreements) and standing settlement instructions.

Counterparty risk is monitored daily against limits; exposure is mitigated by netting, collateral, and central clearing, and limits exist at many levels (counterparty, issuer, sector, country, rating, DV01/CS01, stress-loss, trader authority).

pitfalls: Legal-entity confusion is a classic operational failure: you face a specific legal entity (a subsidiary or branch), not the parent's brand name — the parent may not stand behind the subsidiary.
Wrong-way risk: exposure that grows exactly when the counterparty weakens (e.g. buying protection on a bank from that bank's affiliate).
Soft limits warn and escalate; hard limits block — overrides must be approved and audit-trailed, or the control is theater.

claims.text: Bootstrapping builds a zero (spot) curve from traded par instruments one maturity at a time, reusing the discount factors already pinned down; forward rates are then implied by no-arbitrage between adjacent spot rates.
The G-spread is a bond's yield minus an interpolated government yield; the I-spread swaps the benchmark to the swap curve; both compress a whole bond into one number against one curve point.

The Z-spread is the constant spread added to every point of the benchmark zero curve so the bond's discounted cash flows equal its market dirty price — it accounts for the whole curve shape, not one point.

OAS is the spread after stripping the embedded option's value using a model of rate volatility: OAS = Z-spread − option cost, so a callable bond's OAS is below its Z-spread and a putable bond's is above.

An asset swap packages a fixed-coupon bond with a fixed-for-floating swap so the holder earns floating + the asset-swap spread — a market price for the bond's credit and liquidity risk with the rate risk removed.

Steepeners/flatteners trade the slope between two curve points; butterflies trade curvature (belly vs wings); barbell vs bullet positions the same duration at different curve points; all are expressed and risk-managed in key-rate DV01s.

pitfalls: 'Rich' means expensive (spread too tight / yield too low vs peers) and 'cheap' means the opposite — newcomers reliably invert this.
A wide spread is not free money: it can be compensation for illiquidity, embedded options, or a deteriorating credit the screens have not caught up with.
Basis (cash-futures, CDS-bond) persists for structural reasons — funding, balance-sheet capacity, delivery options, supply/demand — so 'it must converge' trades can bleed for a long time first.

claims.text: Modified duration measures the approximate percentage price change for a 1% (100bp) change in yield; it is a first-order (linear) approximation that is good for small moves only.

DV01 (dollar value of one basis point, also PVBP/PV01) = modified duration × market value / 10,000; it converts rate sensitivity into dollars per basis point and is the standard unit for aggregating and hedging rate risk across bonds, swaps and futures.
A portfolio's rates P&L for a small parallel move is approximately −DV01 × (move in bp): with DV01 of $80,000, a +6bp move loses about $480,000.

Key-rate DV01s split the total DV01 across curve points (2y, 5y, 10y, 30y), measuring exposure to the curve's shape; a net-zero total DV01 can still lose on a steepening if the key rates are mismatched.

Convexity is the curvature the linear duration estimate misses: positive convexity means gaining more / losing less than duration predicts on big moves; callable bonds and MBS have negative convexity from their embedded short options.

Carry is the income from holding (coupon accrual plus pull-to-par, minus funding for a levered position); roll-down is the price gain from sliding to a shorter point on an upward-sloping, unchanged curve; together they are the expected return if nothing moves.
A bond's total P&L decomposes into carry/roll-down (time passing on an unchanged curve), rates P&L (benchmark curve moves), spread P&L (credit spread moves), plus convexity and residual terms.

pitfalls: Duration is in percent, DV01 in dollars — a huge position in a short bond can carry more DV01 than a small position in a long bond.
Carry is not free return: high-carry positions typically embed tail risk (the market charges you nothing for nothing).
Pull-to-par works both ways: premium bonds grind down to 100, discount bonds grind up — forgetting it makes coupon income look like the whole carry.

claims.text: A repo is a sale with agreement to repurchase: economically a collateralized loan where the price difference is the interest; a reverse repo is the lender's side (cash out, securities in).
Haircuts protect the cash lender: lending $98 against $100 of collateral (2%) absorbs collateral price moves; haircut size reflects collateral quality and counterparty creditworthiness.
Repo comes in overnight, term, and open (rolling daily until closed) flavors; tri-party repo outsources collateral selection, valuation and custody to a clearing bank.

Derivatives collateral has two parts: variation margin covers current mark-to-market daily, initial margin covers potential future exposure; cleared trades post both to a CCP, bilateral trades per the CSA.

DVP (delivery versus payment) settlement exchanges securities and cash simultaneously, removing principal risk; a failed delivery is a 'fail', and TMPG's fails charge (up to 3% per annum minus the reference rate) makes failing costly even when rates are near zero.
Fails propagate: a dealer who doesn't receive securities often fails on its own delivery in turn, so one fail can daisy-chain through the market — part of why fails charges and buy-in rights exist.

Funding stress spirals: losses force sales, falling prices raise margins and haircuts, higher haircuts force more sales — Brunnermeier & Pedersen's margin/liquidity spiral, where market liquidity and funding liquidity reinforce each other downward.

pitfalls: A trade that looks attractive on spread can be unattractive after funding: repo cost, haircut (your capital locked up), and the risk the haircut rises are all part of the expected return.
'Off balance sheet' is not 'free': dealer balance-sheet capacity constrains repo intermediation, and that capacity gets expensive exactly in stress.
Margin calls are same-day cash demands; a profitable position can still sink a fund that cannot meet the call (liquidity kills faster than insolvency).

claims.text: An executed price is a real transaction for a specific size and moment; a dealer quote may be executable or indicative; an evaluated price is a vendor's estimate built from observed trades, quotes and models; a composite blends sources; they are different animals and must be labeled as such.

Evaluated pricing services (ICE, Bloomberg BVAL, Refinitiv) rank and combine direct market observations with model-based prices; vendor strengths differ by asset class (one study found ICE leading in governments, BVAL strong in US IG corporates).

Under the fair-value hierarchy, Level 1 is quoted prices in active markets for identical assets; Level 2 is observable inputs (quotes for similar assets, benchmark curves); Level 3 is unobservable model inputs — most bonds priced off evaluated prices land in Level 2.

SR 11-7 defines model risk as the potential for adverse consequences from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs, and requires validation covering conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring, and outcomes analysis, with governance, inventories and audit trails.

Reference data (identifiers, coupon, day count, call schedule, rating, sector) is the skeleton every other system keys off; bad reference data silently corrupts pricing, risk and settlement downstream.

pitfalls: Stale evaluated prices in illiquid bonds smooth reported volatility and hide risk — a portfolio can look calm precisely because nothing in it trades.
Benchmark (on-the-run) liquidity evaporates differently from off-the-run liquidity in stress; bid-ask quoted in normal times says little about exit cost at size in a crisis.
Model governance is not bureaucracy: an unvalidated prepayment or recovery assumption is a position, just an invisible one.

claims.text: The end-to-end walkthrough reuses claims already recorded under cash-flows (dirty price, settlement), orders-axes-execution (RFQ, axes, allocation/affirmation), counterparties-credit-limits (pre-trade checks), curves-spreads-relative-value (spread choice), duration-dv01-convexity (DV01 hedge sizing, P&L decomposition), funding-repo-collateral (repo financing, haircuts, margin), and liquidity-data-models (price types) — see those entries for sources.

Hedging a corporate bond's rate risk with Treasury futures or a swap leaves the credit spread exposure: the hedge removes (approximately) the rates P&L term, so remaining P&L is spread moves + carry/roll + hedge basis.
A DV01-matched hedge is sized as hedge notional = bond DV01 / hedge instrument DV01 per unit; key-rate mismatches between the bond's maturity and the hedge's leave curve risk.

pitfalls: The hedged trade is not riskless: spread widening (the view being expressed) can coincide with funding stress and margin calls on the hedge.
Stress tests should shock the package (bond + hedge + financing) jointly: parallel moves, steepening, spread widening, haircut rises, and a forced-sale scenario.

claims.text: Present value discounts a future cash flow by the rate for its date: PV = CF / (1+r)^t with annual compounding; a discount factor is the PV of $1 at that date, and a bond's price is the sum of its cash flows times their discount factors.

Yield to maturity is the single rate that discounts all of a bond's cash flows to its market (dirty) price — an internal rate of return, quoted per the market's compounding convention (semiannual for US bonds).

Day-count conventions set how much interest accrues between dates: US Treasuries accrue actual/actual, most US corporate bonds 30/360, and money-market instruments actual/360; the convention changes the accrued-interest number for identical dates.
Accrued interest = coupon per period × (days accrued / days in period) under the bond's day-count convention; clean + accrued = dirty.
DV01 = modified duration × market value / 10,000; convexity adds the second-order correction ½ × convexity × (Δy)² that duration misses on larger moves.

Z-spread and OAS are defined against the whole zero curve (constant spread over every point; OAS additionally strips embedded-option value with a volatility model); discount margin is the floating-rate note analogue.

pitfalls: Mixing compounding conventions (annual vs semiannual) when comparing yields silently misquotes by several basis points.
30/360 and actual/360 look interchangeable but are not: actual/360 accrues about 1.4% more interest over a year than the stated rate suggests.
Duration-based P&L estimates degrade on big moves — that is convexity, not a data error.

volatile: SOFR and benchmark-rate plumbing (post-LIBOR conventions are recent and still evolving)
